Texting laughs

hahaha (warm)

use at least three ha's — two reads lukewarm.
Hāhāhā, nǐ tài gǎoxiào le

heh (COLD — landmine)

no longer a laugh — reads sarcastic or dismissive in text. Recognize it, don't send it.
"Wǒ shuō de shì zhēn de."

Glue — grammar

yī…jiù "as soon as A, then B"

Template: yī + V/phrase, jiù + result

instant or automatic link between two events

Wǒ yí xiàbān jiù qù.
Nǐ yí lái jiù zhīdào le.

Foreigner traps

  • The subject sits OUTSIDE the frame: Wǒ yí xiàbān jiù qù, never Yí wǒ xiàbān — yī hugs its verb.
  • Citation yī shifts tone before the event: say yí before a 4th tone (yí dào), yì before 1st/2nd/3rd (yì tiān) — your mouth learns the sandhi from the chunks.
  • Don't stretch it to 'whenever': repeated-habit 'every time A, B' is měi...jiù — yī…jiù is one specific trigger, one immediate result.

hái, the multi-load adverb

Template: hái + V/Adj ("still"); Hái yǒu… ("also/plus"); Hái méi ne ("not yet")

status checks ("still?"), additions, and the default answer to a "le ma?" question

"Wǒ shuō de shì zhēn de."

Foreigner traps

  • freezing hái as dictionary "still" and missing "hái méi ne" as the everyday answer

Native notes — Chongqing answer words, texting culture, and the burnout triad

nānggè and sázi carry a postcode — yours

They're the Chongqing forms of zěnme and shénme, and using them is the single fastest way to sound local instead of 'learned Mandarin from TV'. Keep the textbook twins for neutral-standard moments. Around town you'll also hear the Chengdu twins — zǎgè, mòdé — understand them, don't switch.

Laugh-length is a social signal

In texting, hāhāhā (three or more) is warm; hāhā (two) reads perfunctory or sarcastic to anyone under 35; hēhē is cold, dismissive, sometimes hostile — the classic passive-aggressive reply. If a friend sends hēhē, something is wrong. Matching laugh length to warmth is a real native skill.

The burnout triad is generational membership

nèijuǎn (rat-race competition), tǎngpíng (opting out), bǎilàn (letting it rot) form one story arc natives under 40 use constantly — and juǎn alone works as a verb ('my team juǎns so hard'). Using them accurately signals cultural fluency more than any textbook phrase; overusing them at work signals attitude. They're couch words, not office words.

zài ma? — the dreaded opener

Opening a chat with Zài ma? and nothing else is the classic 'brace yourself' move — natives mildly dread it because it demands commitment before the topic is known. The fluent pattern is to lead with the thing: Gàosu nǐ ge shì, then the news. Ask zài ma only when you need real-time back-and-forth.
